statement: In Texas you file a petition asking for a name change in the Texas county where you live, and a judge signs an order granting it. You must be at least 18 years old.
detail: You get a legible and complete set of your fingerprints taken, and you give the court complete information about all felonies and Class A or B misdemeanors. You file your petition with the district clerk's office in your county. In some counties you also pay for a criminal background check. The signed order is then used to update other documents.

cost.note: The court filing fee may be between $150 and $300 depending on where you live — ask the district clerk's office in your county. If you have a low income you can ask the court to waive the filing fee with a Statement of Inability to Afford Payment of Court Costs. You also pay to be fingerprinted, and in some counties for a criminal background check.

source.title: TexasLawHelp — I Want to Change My Name (Adult Name Change Guide)

statement: To change the name on your Texas driver's license or ID, visit the Department of Public Safety within the required time after your name change, bring your court order and proof of identity, and apply for a corrected card.

topic: Texas driver's license sex marker policy
statement: The Texas State Law Library says the Texas Department of Public Safety in 2024 stopped accepting court orders that change a person's sex, and stopped accepting combined orders that grant a name change and a gender-marker change in the same document.
detail: Texas enacted House Bill 229 in 2025, which defines words like female, male, woman, and man where other laws use them. Attorney General Opinion KP-0489 addresses whether a district court order can direct a state agency to amend a person's sex on a state identification document. The library says it cannot tell you what the law means for your situation. This area is contested and moving — read the official sources before you file anything.

source.title: Texas State Law Library — Gender Marker Change (Name Changes in Texas)

statement: Texas Vital Statistics lists only two documents it will take to correct the sex on a birth certificate: a hospital or medical record from the birth, or a letter from the hospital saying what clerical error it made. It lists no way to change the sex on a Texas birth certificate to match your gender identity.
detail: The same page does take a certified court order for other changes to a birth record, such as a legal name change. It does not list one for the sex field. Read the official page yourself before you file anything. Do not assume a route is open here.

source.title: Texas DSHS Vital Statistics — Supporting Documentation for Record Changes and Corrections

topic: Texas law on sex on state records
statement: The Texas State Law Library says that in 2025 Texas enacted House Bill 229, which defines sex as an individual's biological sex, either male or female, in laws that did not already define it.
detail: The library also points to Attorney General Opinion KP-0489, from March 2025, on whether a district court order can direct a state agency to amend a person's sex on a state ID document. The library says it cannot tell you what the law means for your situation.

source.title: Texas State Law Library — Gender Marker Change (Name Changes in Texas)

statement: To change the legal name on a Texas birth certificate, Texas Vital Statistics asks for a certified copy of a court order affecting the information shown on the birth certificate.
detail: You apply by mail. Get the signed court order first.

source.title: Texas DSHS Vital Statistics — Supporting Documentation for Record Changes and Corrections

statement: Texas lists a $15 fee to correct a birth certificate for most changes, and $22 for a new certified copy of the corrected birth record.
detail: Adding, removing, or replacing a parent costs $25 instead. Fees are not refunded, even if the record is not found.

cost.note: A new certified copy of the corrected record costs $22 more. Fees are not refunded.

source.title: Texas DSHS Vital Statistics — Costs and Fees

topic: Texas name change for a child
statement: TexasLawHelp says a child's name-change case can be filed by the child's parent, managing conservator, or legal guardian. If your child is 10 years old or older, you cannot change your child's name without their consent.
detail: You must tell the other parent about the case, even if that parent is not listed on your child's birth certificate, unless their parental rights have been terminated. If the other parent does not agree, you must have them served with legal notice by a constable, sheriff, or private process server, and you must set a contested final hearing with at least 45 days' notice to that parent. If you cannot find the other parent after looking really hard, you must serve them by publication in a local newspaper, the state's public information website, or both, and you must hire a lawyer to serve as their attorney ad litem. Be prepared to tell the judge why the name change is in the child's best interest.

cost.note: Contact the district clerk's office in the county where the child lives for the filing fee. A low-income parent can ask the court to waive it with a Statement of Inability to Afford Payment of Court Costs.

source.title: TexasLawHelp — I Want to Change My Child's Name
